title: Pattern testing and choke care
summary: How to check your pattern on a plate, how to clean and grease chokes, and why Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting shooters do not fire a multichoke gun without a choke.

body.html: To see what your choke really does, you shoot at a pattern plate: a large steel sheet that is painted or greased so the pellets leave marks. A big sheet of paper, about 1 × 1 m, also works. Do this only at a ground that has such a plate, and with the staff's permission.

To check gun fit you shoot from close range, about 15 m (16 yards): what matters there is where the centre of the pattern is. To judge the choke itself the distance is longer, classically 35 m or 40 yards (about 36.6 m). On paper you draw a circle 75–76 cm across around the densest part and count the pellet holes inside it. Then compare that number with the number of pellets in the cartridge (roughly 350–400 for 28 g of No. 7½; see Shot size).

Roughly, at that distance cylinder puts about 40% of the shot in the circle, improved cylinder about 50%, modified about 60%, improved modified about 65%, and full 70% or more. The figures depend on the cartridge, so your own gun and cartridge may give different results.

One shot proves little: patterns vary noticeably even with identical cartridges. Fire at least 3–5 shots for each combination. Look at evenness too: a good pattern is even, without big holes and without a dense blob in the middle.

html: After shooting, unscrew the chokes with the choke key.
Clean them inside and out with solvent and a brush, and wipe the thread in the muzzle.
Before screwing them back in, put a thin layer of choke grease on the thread: it prevents rust and stops the choke from seizing.

body.html: Check that chokes are tight before each session, because shooting can slowly loosen them. Screw them in fully with the key, but without excessive force.

Never fire a multichoke gun without a choke, or with a choke that is only half screwed in. The shot and the wad can damage the thread in the muzzle, and the repair is expensive. Keep spare chokes in a separate case so they do not get lost.

key_points.html: Patterns are checked on a plate: fit at about 15 m (16 yards), chokes at 35 m or 40 yards.
Count the share of shot in a 75–76 cm circle; fire 3–5 shots.
Clean chokes after shooting and grease the threads with choke grease.
Check that chokes are tight before each session.
Never fire a multichoke gun without a choke.

did_you_know.html: After each shot the pattern plate is painted or greased again, with a roller or brush, so that the next marks do not mix with the previous ones.

quiz.q: Why should you not fire a multichoke gun without a choke?

options.text: It is banned only in competitions
Shot and wad can damage the muzzle thread
The gun will not fire at all then
The pattern becomes far too tight

quiz.explain: Without a choke the thread is exposed, and the shot and wad can damage it.

quiz.q: At what classic distance is a choke's pattern judged?
quiz.explain: The share of shot in a 75–76 cm circle is classically counted at 35 m or 40 yards.

quiz.q: How many shots should you fire to judge a pattern?

options.text: One shot is enough for this
A hundred, on the same day

quiz.explain: Patterns vary from shot to shot, so you need a series for each gun, choke and cartridge.
